CONFIRM C0029 | `run_pyright()` parses only `result.stdout` as JSON. `_run_tool()` captures both streams, and pyright can emit its machine-readable payload on stderr in some environments/wrappers while exiting nonzero for findings. In that path, `json.loads(result.stdout)` sees empty text, logs parse failure, and returns no diagnostics, so health scan silently undercounts type issues and fix evaluation baseline/post counts are wrong.

FINDING_ID: F001
SEVERITY: 0.95
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.74
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` does not actually sandbox multi-file fixes. In `bench/endocrine.py`, it copies only the single target file into a temp directory, writes the patched basename there, then runs pyright/ruff/bandit on that isolated file path. Evidence: `patched_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, os.path.basename(target_path))` and post-fix analysis calls `_count_tool_issues(..., patched_path)`. Any fix whose correctness depends on sibling modules, package layout, imports, or project config is evaluated against a broken one-file world rather than a sandboxed copy of the source tree.
FOLLOW: This crosses the endocrine→immune interface because `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()` uses `evaluate_fixes()` to mark surviving findings as `verified=True` when verdict is SAFE or NEUTRAL. In the current design, a fix can be marked SAFE merely because isolated-file checks miss project-level breakage, import failures, or cross-module type regressions. That incorrectly activates the NK bug-closed gate in later rounds, causing real bugs to be treated as CLOSED and deduplicated away. The inverse also happens: valid fixes can be judged HARMFUL/UNEVALUABLE because imports fail in the fake one-file sandbox, so reviewers see misleading fix-eval output and the PoC’s “programmatic verification” feature does not fire reliably end-to-end.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — copy the relevant source tree into the temp directory, preserve relative paths, apply the patch to the target file inside that copied tree, and run pyright/ruff/bandit from the temp project root against the patched relative path. Do not evaluate against a lone basename file.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F002
SEVERITY: 0.92
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.71
DESCRIPTION: FIND — test execution in `evaluate_fix()` is not sandbox-correct and often does not test the patched code. The function runs the caller-supplied `test_cmd` unchanged with only `cwd=tmpdir`. In context, the immune pipeline passes `["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", "-x", "-q", "--tb=no", "--no-header", "-q"]`. Because only one patched file is placed in `tmpdir` and the command still references the original `bench/tests/` path and default import resolution, pytest will typically import the real source tree outside the tempdir, not the patched file. So “tests_passed” is not evidence about the sandboxed fix.
FOLLOW: Downstream, `_compute_fix_verdict()` treats passing tests as SAFE when issue counts are unchanged, and immune stage 4 sets `verified=True` for SAFE or NEUTRAL fixes. That means a fix can be programmatically “verified” even though no test exercised the patched code. This directly corrupts the verification signal used by the immune pipeline and later duplicate-closing logic, producing silently wrong reviewer-facing verdicts about fix safety.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — rewrite test execution to run against the copied temp project: copy the project subtree, execute tests from that temp root, and rewrite or reject `test_cmd` arguments that point outside the sandbox. If that cannot be guaranteed, set `tests_passed=None` and do not treat test success as evidence.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.88
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_compute_fix_verdict()` can classify regressions as SAFE because it sums net issue deltas across tools and only checks `total_net > 0`. Example from code: `total_net = net_type + net_ruff + net_bandit`; if one new pyright error is introduced and two ruff warnings disappear, `total_net == -1`, so the verdict becomes SAFE. That is logically wrong for “no new issues introduced”: a fix that adds any new type or security issue should not be safe merely because unrelated lint count dropped more.
FOLLOW: This affects the core endocrine capability “Fix evaluation — SAFE/HARMFUL/NEUTRAL.” The immune pipeline trusts SAFE/NEUTRAL to set `verified=True`. Under current logic, fixes that introduce new type or security defects can be marked SAFE, then propagated into canonical findings as verified fixes, which closes bugs prematurely and misleads the human reviewer about source health.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — mark the result HARMFUL if any individual net metric is positive (`net_type_errors > 0 or net_ruff_errors > 0 or net_bandit_issues > 0`); only consider SAFE when all are `<= 0` and at least one is `< 0` or tests pass.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F004
SEVERITY: 0.72
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `scan_health()` advertises “Tool availability (tool -> bool)” but omits keys for tools when no exception is raised and the runner internally returns `[]` for missing binary or timeout. Evidence: each runner returns `[]` on `"NOT_FOUND"`; `scan_health()` then sets `tools_available[tool_name] = True` after normal return. Even after existing registry fixes for missing-tool truthiness, the shape is still inconsistent when early-return/parse-failure cases happen: callers cannot distinguish “tool unavailable,” “tool timed out,” and “tool ran cleanly” from the boolean map alone.
FOLLOW: This weakens the insect-brain-facing health signal. The brain receives a HealthScan that looks structurally complete but lacks trustworthy per-tool status semantics, so reviewers can misread an empty diagnostic set as healthy code rather than partial scan coverage. It also makes future trend logic or UI summaries unable to reason about tool health consistently.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — populate `tools_available` deterministically for every configured tool and derive the boolean from explicit runner status, not from exception/no-exception. Missing, timeout, and parse-failed runs should all set the tool key present with `False`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

EXTEND C0004 | Evidence is not limited to missing binaries. The same false-positive “available” status occurs for timeout and parse-failure paths because `scan_health()` treats any normal runner return as availability. Since runners currently collapse NOT_FOUND/TIMEOUT/empty-unparseable output into `[]`, the health scan can report a tool as available with zero diagnostics even when it never produced usable output. The fix needs explicit execution status propagation, not just a binary-exists check.

EXTEND C0021 | Timeout mishandling also corrupts fix evaluation, not just health scan. `_count_tool_issues()` calls the same runners on pre/post files; when a tool times out, the runner returns `[]`, so baseline and post counts become zero and `_compute_fix_verdict()` can classify the fix SAFE/NEUTRAL despite the checker never completing. The downstream consequence is false `verified=True` in immune stage 4.

EXTEND C0005 | The dead-feature problem is broader on fix evaluation: the module docstring promises “sandboxed (tempdir, never modifies actual source),” but the current implementation is only single-file temp output plus unchanged external test command. So the advertised new capability exists nominally but does not reliably fire on real project-shaped fixes.

EXTEND C0003 | There is additional incompleteness beyond unused defect categories: whole advertised tooling paths are declared but not wired into health or fix evaluation. `MYPY_BIN` is scanned, but `crosshair` and `python3.13` are declared as tool binaries in the public module contract and never participate in any emitted report or evaluation path. This is another example of interface promises exceeding implemented behavior.
